description: melissa khair, a student at BEA
summary: VITALS is a health self‑check and care guide that helps astronauts when a doctor can be 20 minutes away. VITALS has two parts: Astronauts and Ship. When an astronaut logs in VITALS quietly measures how precise a tap is and how fast a keyboard rhythm is, to see if the astronaut is alert. The top bar contains a search bar, a Near Earth/Mars toggle a Health alert that asks if the astronaut is OK and will notify the crew after 30 seconds if no reply comes and a Get Help button that starts a symptom survey and then connects the astronaut to a doctor or gives step‑by‑step help. The crew overview shows each astronaut’s status, alerts and a shared day plan. Each astronaut’s console holds a sonar‑style sound scan for breathing and heart rate an ultrasound bone scan, voice mood detection, a body coloured by health status and an eight‑question check‑in that creates an AI daily schedule. Readings get better as treatment steps are finished and get worse when steps are ignored. The Ship part shows a spacecraft with live air and radiation data for each room an entry log, an equipment inventory, a supply forecast and interactive emergencies. Ship events change crew health medicine used reduces ship stock and every reading is compared with the astronaut’s normal from, before launch using NASA methods.
details:
VITALS is a browser-based health self-check and care guide designed for astronauts on missions where a doctor's 20 minutes away in each direction. It collects health data in everyday ways. At login it reads tap and typing patterns. Each morning the astronaut answers eight questions. It uses a sonar-style sound scan that listens to the echo of a tone to measure breathing and heart rate. It also includes an ultrasound bone scan, voice mood analysis and eye photos that are only taken when the astronaut wants them. There is a patch and a smart bathroom but in the prototype both are simulated.

Every health reading is compared to the astronaut’s normal levels from before launch. The results show up as Nominal, Caution or Warning on a body model. The system gives step-by-step treatment advice, prevention tips and an AI-powered daily schedule that fits what the astronaut can safely do.

There is also a Ship section that shows air quality, radiation, supplies and emergencies in 3D. Events on the ship can affect the crews health readings. This system helps with detection of health problems. It supports self-care without waiting for help from Earth. It takes little time from the crew. It sends alerts automatically if an astronaut does not respond. All health and supply information is in one place.

The goal is to support Earth-independent medical care on the ISS, the Moon and Mars. It can also help people far from doctors on Earth—like those at stations on ships or in remote clinics.

We built VITALS using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. We used three.js for the 3D visuals the Web Audio API for sensing and Canvas for live graphs. We tested it with Playwright. We used Canva for the presentation. We also used an AI coding assistant named Claude to help build and test it.

VITALS runs on any laptop or tablet that has a speaker, microphone and camera. The smart patch and smart bathroom are simulated in the prototype.

This system is creative because it turns a tablet’s speaker into a contact- sensor. It checks alertness invisibly during login. It shows recovery in time as the astronaut follows treatment. It links ship emergencies to crew health. It compares a doctor on Earth with VITALS guiding the astronaut alone on the way to Mars.

Our team thought about astronauts’ schedules. We considered privacy. We made sure it was accessible. We accounted for communication delays, with Earth. We followed NASA science.. We kept the design simple without hiding the system’s depth.
